vibrations.natural_frequency.title: Undamped natural frequency, cyclic frequency and period
assumptions: Undamped single degree of freedom. omega_n is in rad/s and f_n = omega_n/(2 pi) in Hz (the 2 pi is the physical angular/cyclic relation, not a unit conversion).
method_references: omega_n = sqrt(k/m); f_n = omega_n/(2 pi); T = 1/f_n

vibrations.equiv_stiffness.title: Equivalent stiffness of two springs in series or parallel

variables.name: k_parallel
variables.desc: equivalent stiffness in parallel (k = sum k_i)

method_references: Series: 1/k_eq = 1/k1 + 1/k2; parallel: k_eq = k1 + k2

vibrations.equiv_mass.title: Equivalent mass of a spring-mass system (spring mass correction)
assumptions: Approximate Rayleigh correction for a spring of uniform mass: one third of the spring mass acts at the free end.
method_references: m_eq = m + m_spring/3 (Rayleigh spring-mass correction, recalled)

vibrations.damping.title: Damping ratio and critical damping coefficient
assumptions: zeta < 1 underdamped, = 1 critically damped, > 1 overdamped.
method_references: c_c = 2 sqrt(k m) = 2 m omega_n; zeta = c/c_c

vibrations.log_decrement.title: Logarithmic decrement and damped natural frequency
assumptions: Underdamped only (zeta < 1). delta is the natural log of the ratio of two successive same-side peak amplitudes.
method_references: delta = 2 pi zeta / sqrt(1 - zeta^2); omega_d = omega_n sqrt(1 - zeta^2)

vibrations.free_response.title: Free-vibration amplitude and phase from initial conditions
assumptions: Underdamped free response x(t) = A e^{-zeta omega_n t} cos(omega_d t - phi) with omega_d = omega_n sqrt(1 - zeta^2) derived from zeta and omega_n.
method_references: A and phi from the initial displacement and velocity of an underdamped oscillator

vibrations.forced_response.title: Forced steady-state response: magnification factor, amplitude and phase
assumptions: Harmonic force F0 sin(omega t); steady-state response at the forcing frequency. M peaks near r = 1 (resonance). The phase lag phi is atan2(2 zeta r, 1 - r^2).
method_references: Steady-state forced response of an SDOF oscillator

vibrations.transmissibility.title: Force transmissibility and isolation efficiency
assumptions: Force transmitted through the mount to the foundation. Isolation (TR < 1) requires r > sqrt(2); eta < 0 below that means amplification.

vibrations.rotating_unbalance_response.title: Steady-state response to a rotating unbalance
assumptions: Rotating unbalance m_e at radius e. X -> m_e e/M as r -> infinity (independent of damping there).
method_references: X = (m_e e/M) r^2 / sqrt((1 - r^2)^2 + (2 zeta r)^2) (recalled)

vibrations.base_excitation.title: Response to harmonic base (support) excitation: absolute and relative displacement

variables.name: X
variables.desc: absolute displacement amplitude of the mass

variables.name: Z
variables.desc: relative displacement amplitude between mass and base

assumptions: X is the ABSOLUTE displacement amplitude of the mass; Z is the relative displacement amplitude between the mass and the base. |X|/Y equals the force transmissibility; |Z|/Y = r^2/sqrt((1 - r^2)^2 + (2 zeta r)^2).
method_references: Base-excitation absolute response X/Y = sqrt((1 + (2 zeta r)^2)/((1 - r^2)^2 + (2 zeta r)^2)) and relative response Z/Y = r^2/sqrt((1 - r^2)^2 + (2 zeta r)^2)

vibrations.mdof.title: Multi-degree-of-freedom natural frequencies and mode shapes

variables.name: modes
variables.desc: mode shape vectors: modes[j] is the j-th mode vector (mass-normalized)

assumptions: Undamped, symmetric, positive-definite M and K. Solves the generalized eigenproblem K phi = omega^2 M phi; modes are mass-normalized (phi^T M phi = 1), signs arbitrary.
method_references: Generalized eigenproblem K phi = omega^2 M phi (scipy.linalg.eigh)

vibrations.absorber_tuning.title: Tuned dynamic vibration absorber stiffness

variables.name: omega
variables.desc: disturbing frequency to cancel (enter rad/s or rpm)
variables.label: ω

assumptions: The absorber is tuned so its own natural frequency sqrt(k_a/m_a) equals the disturbing frequency omega; at that frequency the main mass stays still.
method_references: Absorber tuning k_a = m_a omega^2 (Frahm absorber)

vibrations.absorber_frequencies.title: Natural frequencies of a main mass with an attached absorber

variables.name: omega1
variables.desc: lower natural frequency of the combined system
variables.label: ω1

variables.name: omega2
variables.desc: upper natural frequency of the combined system
variables.label: ω2

procedure.python:
def _absorber_frequencies(values):
    """Natural frequencies of a main mass m (spring k) with a tuned/attached absorber m_a, k_a.

    Roots of m m_a omega^4 - [k m_a + k_a (m + m_a)] omega^2 + k k_a = 0 (det of [K - omega^2 M])."""
    m, k, ma, ka = values['m'], values['k'], values['m_a'], values['k_a']
    A = m * ma
    Bc = k * ma + ka * (m + ma)
    C = k * ka
    disc = Bc * Bc - 4.0 * A * C
    if disc < 0.0:
        raise MechError('negative discriminant (check the input units)')
    Om1 = (Bc - math.sqrt(disc)) / (2.0 * A)
    Om2 = (Bc + math.sqrt(disc)) / (2.0 * A)
    return {'omega1': math.sqrt(Om1), 'omega2': math.sqrt(Om2)}

assumptions: Undamped two-degree-of-freedom system; the two frequencies bracket the tuned absorber frequency (the disturbing frequency should be kept off these peaks).
method_references: Characteristic equation det([K - omega^2 M]) = 0 for main + absorber masses

vibrations.torsional_vibration.title: Torsional natural frequency of a shaft-disk system

variables.name: I
variables.desc: mass moment of inertia of the disk

assumptions: Massless shaft, single rigid disk; free (undamped) torsional vibration.
method_references: k_t = GJ/L; omega_n = sqrt(k_t/I)

vibrations.critical_speed_shaft.title: Shaft critical speed from static deflection (single disk)

variables.name: delta_st
variables.desc: static deflection under the disk weight

assumptions: Single disk (any location along the shaft), weight-loaded; omega_cr = sqrt(g/delta_st) with delta_st the static deflection under the disk. To get rpm, convert the rad/s result. For several disks use rayleigh or dunkerley.
method_references: omega_cr = sqrt(g/delta_st)

vibrations.rayleigh.title: Rayleigh's method: first critical speed from static deflections

variables.name: masses
variables.desc: rows [W (N), y (m)]: each load and its static deflection

assumptions: Rayleigh energy method with the static-deflection curve as the assumed mode; gives an upper bound on the fundamental critical speed.
method_references: Rayleigh's method: omega_cr^2 = g sum(W y)/sum(W y^2)

vibrations.dunkerley.title: Dunkerley's method: first critical speed from individual speeds

variables.name: speeds
variables.desc: individual critical speeds (rad/s), one per load acting alone

assumptions: Dunkerley's method: 1/omega_cr^2 = sum 1/omega_i^2; gives a lower bound on the fundamental critical speed.
method_references: Dunkerley's reciprocal formula 1/omega_cr^2 = sum 1/omega_i^2

vibrations.string_frequency.title: Natural frequencies of a taut string
assumptions: Flexible string, small amplitude, both ends fixed; n is the harmonic number.
method_references: omega_n = (n pi/L) sqrt(T/mu)

vibrations.bar_longitudinal.title: Longitudinal natural frequencies of a bar (fixed-fixed)
assumptions: Longitudinal (axial) vibration, fixed-fixed or free-free (same frequencies). A fixed-free bar gives f_n = (2n - 1)/(4L) sqrt(E/rho) instead.
method_references: omega_n = (n pi/L) sqrt(E/rho) for a bar in longitudinal vibration

vibrations.beam_frequency.title: Beam natural frequency from numerically found betaL roots

variables.name: bc
variables.desc: boundary condition: pinned-pinned, fixed-free, fixed-fixed or free-free

variables.name: betaL
variables.desc: beta_n L root of the characteristic equation (dimensionless)

assumptions: Uniform Euler-Bernoulli beam; betaL roots are found by root-finding the characteristic equation (not tabulated). Pinned-pinned betaL = n pi is closed form; fixed-free cos(betaL) cosh(betaL) = -1; fixed-fixed/free-free cos(betaL) cosh(betaL) = 1. omega_n = beta^2 sqrt(EI/(rho A)).
method_references: Euler-Bernoulli beam frequency equation; omega_n = beta_n^2 sqrt(EI/(rho A)) with beta_n L the roots of the boundary-condition characteristic equation

vibrations.quality_factor.title: Quality factor and half-power bandwidth
assumptions: Light damping: Q = 1/(2 zeta) relates damping to the resonance sharpness; the half-power bandwidth is omega_n/Q = 2 zeta omega_n.
method_references: Q = 1/(2 zeta); half-power bandwidth = omega_n/Q

vibrations.duhamel.title: Shock/transient response by the Duhamel (convolution) integral

variables.name: forces
variables.desc: force values (N) at each time point

variables.name: response
variables.desc: displacement response x(t) at each time point (m)

variables.name: x_max
variables.desc: extreme (peak) response: the sample with the largest |x|, signed

procedure.python:
def _duhamel(values):
    """Response of an underdamped SDOF system to a force history via the Duhamel (convolution) integral.

    times and forces are equal-length json lists (s and N). The force history is treated as
    piecewise-constant between the given time points (a zero-order hold) and the response is built by
    superposition of the exact unit-step response h(t) = (1/k)[1 - e^{-zeta wn t}(cos(wd t) +
    (zeta wn/wd) sin(wd t))], i.e. x(t) = sum_j (F_j - F_{j-1}) h(t - t_j). This is exact for a
    zero-order-hold force history (and for a step input) and accurate for smooth histories sampled finely."""
    import numpy as np
    m, k, zeta = values['m'], values['k'], values['zeta']
    t = np.asarray(values['times'], float)
    F = np.asarray(values['forces'], float)
    if t.ndim != 1 or F.ndim != 1 or len(t) != len(F):
        raise MechError('times and forces must be equal-length lists')
    if len(t) < 2:
        raise MechError('need at least two time points')
    if zeta < 0.0 or zeta >= 1.0:
        raise MechError('Duhamel integral here covers underdamped systems (0 <= zeta < 1)')
    if np.any(np.diff(t) <= 0.0):
        raise MechError('times must be strictly increasing')
    wn = math.sqrt(k / m)
    wd = wn * math.sqrt(1.0 - zeta * zeta)
    coef = zeta * wn / wd

    def step_resp(tau):
        if tau < 0.0:
            return 0.0
        e = math.exp(-zeta * wn * tau)
        return (1.0 - e * (math.cos(wd * tau) + coef * math.sin(wd * tau))) / k

    resp = []
    for i in range(len(t)):
        ti = t[i]
        x = 0.0
        prevF = 0.0
        for j in range(i + 1):
            dF = F[j] - prevF
            if dF != 0.0:
                x += dF * step_resp(ti - t[j])
            prevF = F[j]
        resp.append(float(x))
    # Extreme response = the sample with the largest |x|, reported with its sign and time.
    i_max = max(range(len(resp)), key=lambda i: abs(resp[i]))
    x_max = resp[i_max]
    t_max = float(t[i_max])
    return {'response': resp, 'x_max': x_max, 't_max': t_max}

assumptions: Underdamped SDOF at rest initially; the force history is a zero-order hold (piecewise constant between time points) superposed with the exact unit-step response. For a suddenly applied constant force the peak response is twice the static deflection (2 F0/k) — a useful check.
method_references: Duhamel integral: x(t) = (1/(m omega_d)) integral_0^t F(tau) e^{-zeta omega_n (t-tau)} sin(omega_d (t-tau)) dtau

Z is the RELATIVE displacement between mass and base: Z = Y r^2/sqrt((1-r^2)^2+(2 zeta r)^2) = 0.002*4/3.006659 = 0.002*1.330384 = 0.002660760 m = 2.660760 mm (|Z|/Y = r^2/sqrt((1-r^2)^2+(2 zeta r)^2)).
